capabilities.target: private repositories owned by the user
pull request on the public repository

inputs.source: Direct chat instruction from the authenticated user
Issues opened in the public repository by any GitHub user

elements.name: Public issue content entering agent context
Pull request creation on public repo

controls.name: Per-tool-call approval prompt
controls.decay_rationale: The approver sees a collapsed, model-generated summary rather than raw arguments, so a more persuasive model can write a more convincing description of a malicious call (ASI09). Approval volume is high (many calls approved per session), producing consent fatigue (SAFE-T1403) that erodes scrutiny further.

controls.name: Least-privilege token scoped to the public repository only
Pin MCP server image to a verified digest
Raw-action, low-volume approval gate for cross-repo and public writes
Cross-repo content check on outbound pull requests
controls.decay_rationale: A content-similarity classifier can be defeated by encoding, paraphrasing, or splitting leaked content across multiple PRs, so it narrows the path rather than closing it.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1): issue-injected instructions cause private repo exfiltration via public pull request

attack_path.note: Any GitHub user can open an issue in the public repo and embed instructions for the agent.
Agent follows the injected instructions and reads confidential files from a private repository using the single broad PAT.
Agent opens a pull request on the public repository containing the private content, publicly disclosing it.

threat_refs.name: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation

forecast.watch_signal: Approval mode changes from per-call prompt to 'always allow'; the client's underlying model is upgraded without re-review; or approvals-per-reviewer-per-day rises further.

evidence.observation: A single GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN with repo scope is passed to the server, covering both public and private repositories.

'Anyone on GitHub can open issues in the public repository' establishes the untrusted source; 'Arguments are collapsed by default' and 'Users approve many calls per session' establish a weak, high-volume approval gate.

recommendations.action: Use a least-privilege token scoped only to the public repository for issue-triage tasks; keep any private-repo token separate and never loaded for this workflow.
Switch the approval prompt to raw-action review (full arguments and destination visible, not collapsed) and keep volume low enough for individual review.
Block create_pull_request calls whose content overlaps with data just read from a different, especially private, repository in the same session.

findings.title: ASI04 supply chain: unpinned github-mcp-server image enables a rug pull to redefine tools or harvest the broad PAT

attack_path.note: The docker image is pulled with no version tag or digest, so the running server binary can change between runs without the user's awareness.
A swapped or compromised server could silently alter what get_file_contents returns or does, including reading beyond what it reports.
A swapped or compromised server could use the same broad PAT to create public PRs, or exfiltrate the PAT itself, independent of any issue content.

threat_refs.name: AI Supply Chain Compromise: AI Agent Tool

forecast.watch_signal: The image reference in mcpServers config changes, or no digest pin is ever added; approval review mode or volume weakens further.

evidence.observation: Image reference 'ghcr.io/github/github-mcp-server' carries no tag or digest, so docker run resolves and can silently change which build executes.

recommendations.action: Pin the server image to a specific digest (sha256) and verify it before each run.

findings.title: No attributable record separating agent actions from human-approved actions

forecast.watch_signal: Agent is given broader autonomy (A3/A4) or connected to additional repos or organizations without a durable, tamper-evident action log being added.

evidence.observation: The artifacts describe an approval prompt and token scope but make no mention of any logging or audit trail attributing actions to the agent versus a human, or preserving them tamper-evidently.

recommendations.action: Maintain a durable, tamper-evident log of every tool call (actor, arguments, approval decision, timestamp) separate from anything the model can edit.

stride_coverage.rationale: This is a single-user desktop process spawned locally by the user's own client; there is no remote identity for another party to spoof.
Every tool call requires a human approval click, which structurally bounds the rate of agent actions to human reaction time for this single-user desktop tool.
The server is spawned locally via docker by the user's own client over stdio; there is no network identity to spoof in this transport.
Every tool call requires a human approval click, which structurally bounds the rate of agent actions to human reaction time for this single-user desktop tool.
This flow carries issue text inbound into the agent's context; it does not itself carry data outside the trust boundary.
Processing of issue content is gated by the same per-call human approval that bounds the rate of downstream agent actions.
This outbound flow is an agent-initiated API call to GitHub over TLS; no third party can tamper with it in transit.
Pull request creation requires a human approval click per call, which bounds the rate of this action for this single-user desktop tool.
Any GitHub user opening an issue in a public repository is legitimate platform behavior, not identity spoofing of another party.
The artifacts do not describe whether GitHub's own issue-authorship records are used to attribute the source of injected content.
The assessed design grants only get_file_contents (read) on private repositories; no write capability to this store is declared.
Reads from this store require a human approval click per call, which bounds the rate of access for this single-user desktop tool.

rating.rationale: A single broadly-scoped PAT covers both public and private repositories, and anyone can open an issue in the public repo that the agent will read. That untrusted content can direct the agent to read confidential private-repo data and then publish it via a public pull request (TC1 lethal trifecta), which is critical inherently. The only control is a per-call approval prompt that shows a collapsed, model-generated summary and is approved at high volume per session, which earns only one tier of credit (rubric 5 step 2), leaving residual at high. An unpinned MCP server image adds an independent critical path (ASI04 rug pull) under the same weak gate. Under model_upgrade, autonomy_increase, or control_removal, that approval gate is the control most likely to fail first (ASI09, SAFE-T1403), returning both findings to critical. A missing audit trail is recorded separately but stays low because it affects an otherwise well-scoped read/write pair rather than adding new reachable harm.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration in the provided artifacts, not observed runtime behavior; no live traffic, logs, or tool outputs were reviewed.
No system prompt or orchestration logic was provided beyond the MCP server configuration and runtime notes; autonomy level and approval wiring are inferred from the runtime notes alone.

The exact sensitivity of data in the user's private repositories and the precise approval volume per reviewer are not stated; data_sensitivity, approval_volume, and likelihood values are best estimates from the available description.
